newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Ogata wants to speed resettlement of boat people.
newsitem.headline: Ogata wants to speed resettlement of boat people.

text.p: The head of the United Nations refugee agency called on Sunday for the resettlement of Vietnamese boat people to be speeded up.

"I think we have to accelerate resettlement for those refugees that have been screened and this is an appeal I will make to donors," UNHCR chief Sadako Ogata told reporters told reporters after a visit to Hong Kong's Pillar Point camp.
Ogata said living conditions of the Vietnamese boat people in Hong Kong camps were not as bad as those of displaced persons in other parts of the world.
"I've seen camps all over the world, many, many camps and I think it is not bad (here). People are free to earn money, which is an enormous advantage," she said.
Ogata arrived in Hong Kong on Sunday for a three-day mission to assess the plight of the territory's Vietnamese refugees.
Her arrival coincided with the release of a scathing report on the camps by Human Rights Watch Asia, which charged that conditions at the detention centers were bad and getting worse.
The Hong Kong government said the report was "groundless" and called its findings "absolute rubbish."

A spokeswoman for Human Rights Watch Asia told Hong Kong government radio that the report was based on the government's own statistics as well as on interviews with people familiar with the camps, including inmates.
She acknowledged that the rights group had not visited the camps, but blamed this on the government's delay in granting access.
Ogata spent part of the day chatting through an interpreter with Vietnamese living at the Pillar Point camp, mostly women with young children.
One mother who had been in Hong Kong detention centers for 10 years told reporters she did not expect to be able to stay after the territory returns to China later this year.

China has told the departing British administration it must empty the camps before Hong Kong's reversion to China at midnight on June 30, though Beijing has not publically stated what steps it would take if Britain misses the deadline.
Britain has had difficulty complying with China's wishes because Vietman has refused to take back thousands of migrants.

On Saturday, Hong Kong Secretary for Security Peter Lai announced that the territory had been forced to make provisions to continue paying for the upkeep of Vietnamese asylum seekers beyond the handover.
Lai said the Hong Kong government had budgeted some HK$137 million (US$17.7 million) for caring for the refugees.
About 5,500 Vietnamese refugees remain in Hong Kong, the last of the tens of thousands that fled their homeland after the communist victory in 1975, often in flimsy boats.
Only about 2,500 of these have been granted the right of return by Vietnam.
Of the rest, about 1,000 are stranded because they do not have "household" documents proving they had a home in Vietnam.
Others have been refused because while they had previously lived in Vietnam, they are ethnic Chinese.

Hong Kong plans to ask Ogata to step up efforts to resettle the boat people and urge Vietnam to take them back. She is scheduled to meet with Governor Chris Patten, Chief-Executive designate Tung Chee-hwa and members of the Legislative Council.
Ogata also faces the long-unresolved issue of the HK$1 billion (US$129 million) the UNHCR owes to the local government for the cost of running its refugee operations here.
